intro: Where are you right now? In a room. In a building. On a street. In a city or a town. In the state of Illinois. In the United States. On planet Earth. A map can show every one of those places.

In this unit you will learn to read a map and to make one. You will learn the four directions. You will find Chicago and Illinois on a globe. Then you will look at the land and water around you: hills, plains, rivers and one very big lake.
You will also see how weather changes what we wear and do. You will see how people change places, and how places change people. And you will learn ways to take care of the place where you live.
bigQuestion: How do maps and places help us understand where we live?

timeline.t: The class hides a treasure and draws a map of the room from above.
The class adds a key: a star means treasure, a square means desk.
The class walks the halls and draws a map of the whole school.
Everyone finds north by watching where the sun comes up.
The class spins a globe and finds the United States, Illinois and Chicago.
Nia's family drives south from Chicago and watches the land go flat.
At the farm, Nia sees fields of corn where prairie grass once grew.
The weather turns cold. Coats and mittens come out of the closet.
The class picks up litter in the park and plants a tree.

words.d: a drawing of a place as seen from above
the list on a map that tells what each symbol means
the direction at the top of most maps
a round model of Earth
the path you take from one place to another
a big piece of flat land
water with land all around it
one of the four parts of the year: winter, spring, summer, fall

test.q: A map shows a place the way who sees it?
test.why: A map is a drawing of a place from above, like a bird's view.

test.q: On the class treasure map, what stood for treasure?
test.why: The key said: star means treasure. Square meant desk.

test.q: On most maps, north is at the…
test.why: On most maps, north is at the top and south is at the bottom.

test.q: On a globe, most of Earth is what color?
test.why: There is more water than land on Earth, so most of a globe is blue.
Chicago is a city inside Illinois. Illinois is a state inside the United States.

test.q: Which is water that flows in a long, thin path?
test.why: A river flows from high land to low land in a long, thin path.
Illinois is mostly flat. It was prairie and is now mostly farmland.

test.q: What do people in Chicago wear in January?
test.why: January in Chicago is cold and snowy, so people dress warm.

test.q: Which shows a place shaping people?
choices: A town by the sea has many fishers
test.why: The sea is right there, so people become fishers. The place shaped their jobs.

test.q: Why should we keep trash out of Lake Michigan?
test.why: Lake Michigan gives Chicago its drinking water. Clean water is for everyone.

write.prompt: Draw a map of the route from your classroom door to one place in your school. Then write: My map helps a new student because... Use the key, a direction word and one thing they pass.
tips: Say what your map helps someone do. That is your claim.
Point to your key and your symbols. That is your evidence.
Tell how the symbols and directions get the new student there. That is your reasoning.
Ask a friend to try your map. If they get lost, fix the map.

title: Maps and Places

chapters.title: Where Things Are
chapters.bigQuestion: How can a drawing help us find our way?

story.title: The Treasure Map
story.kicker: The class hid a treasure. Now they must draw a map so a friend can find it.
paragraphs: Room 12 is quiet. Ms. Ortiz holds up a small gold box. "This is our treasure," she says. "Jamal will hide it. Then we will draw a map. The map will show Priya where it is." Priya waits in the hall.

Jamal hides the box under the reading rug. Now the class draws. They draw the room as if they were birds looking down. A big square is the rug. Small squares are the desks. A long shape is the teacher's table.
Sofia draws a star where the box is. Leo draws a little door. Ms. Ortiz writes a key on the side. It says: star means treasure. Square means desk. Now the map is done.
Priya comes in. She looks at the map. She finds the door. She finds the desks. She walks to the big square. She lifts the rug. There is the gold box! The map worked.
story.think: What did the class draw on the map? What did they leave out?

lessons.title: Looking Down on a Room
lessons.mainIdea: A map is a drawing of a place as seen from above.
reading: Think of a bird. It flies over your classroom. It looks down. It sees the tops of the desks. It sees the top of the rug. It does not see the legs of the chairs. It sees the room from above.
A *map* is a drawing of a place from above. It shows where things are. A map of your room shows the desks, the door and the rug. It shows them the way a bird sees them.
A map is not a photo. It is simpler. It leaves out small things. It keeps the big things. That makes it easy to read.

words.d: a drawing of a place as seen from above

look.title: Your Desk From Above
look.text: Look at your desk. Now stand up. Look down at it. You see the top. You see a book. You see a pencil. You do not see the legs. That is how a map sees things.
look.prompt: What would you draw if you made a map of your desk?

check.q: A map shows a place from where?
choices: From the side, like a photo
check.why: A map is a drawing of a place from above. It shows things the way a bird sees them.

check.q: What would a map of a room show?
choices: Where the desks and rug are
check.why: A map shows where things are. From above, you see the tops of desks and the rug.

check.q: Why is a map easier to read than a photo?
check.why: A map is simpler than a photo. It keeps the big things and leaves out the small things.

lessons.title: The Map Key
lessons.mainIdea: A map key tells what each symbol on a map means.
reading: Look at the treasure map. There is a star on it. What does the star mean? You cannot tell. So the class made a *key*. The key says: star means treasure. Now you know.
A *symbol* is a small picture that stands for something. A square can stand for a desk. A star can stand for treasure. A wavy line can stand for water. Symbols keep the map simple.
The key is a list. It shows each symbol. Next to it, it says what the symbol means. Always read the key first. Then you can read the map.

words.d: a small picture that stands for something on a map
the list on a map that tells what each symbol means

look.title: A Key for the Playground
look.text: A map of the playground has three symbols. A circle. A triangle. A long line. The key says: circle means swing. Triangle means slide. Long line means fence. Now look at the map. There are two circles by the fence.
look.prompt: What is by the fence on this playground?

check.q: What does a map key do?
choices: It tells what each symbol means
check.why: The key is a list of symbols. It tells what each one stands for.

check.q: On the class map, a star stands for what?
check.why: The class wrote the key. It said: star means treasure.

check.q: What should you read first on a map?
check.why: Read the key first. Then you know what every symbol on the map means.

lessons.title: Bigger and Bigger Maps
lessons.mainIdea: A map can show a room, a school or a whole neighborhood.
reading: A map can show a small place. Your room. A map can show a bigger place. Your whole school. On a school map, each room is a small box. The gym is a big box. The hall is a long line.
A map can show a *neighborhood*. That is the streets and homes around your school. On this map, the school is one small box. The streets are lines. The park is a green shape.
The bigger the place, the smaller each thing looks. On the room map, your desk is a square. On the school map, your whole room is a square. On the neighborhood map, the school is a square.

words.d: the streets, homes and stores around a place

look.title: How Many Squares on Each Map?
look.prompt: The neighborhood map has 40 squares. What might each square be?

check.q: On a school map, what is each room?
check.why: On a school map, each room is a small box. The hall is a long line.

check.q: What does a neighborhood map show?
choices: The streets and homes around the school
check.why: A neighborhood is the streets and homes around a place. The map shows all of them.

check.q: As a map shows a bigger place, each thing looks…
check.why: The bigger the place, the smaller each thing looks. A whole school can be one square.

lessons.title: Near, Far, Left and Right
lessons.mainIdea: Words like near, far, left and right tell where a thing is.
reading: Priya looks at the treasure map. The star is *near* the rug. It is *far* from the door. Near means close. Far means a long way off. These words help her find the box.
Left and right help too. Hold up your left hand. Now your right hand. On the map, the door is on the left. The windows are on the right. Priya walks to the right side of the room.
Use these words when you give directions. "The book is near the sink." "The ball is far from the fence." "Turn left at the door." Then a friend can find the way.

words.d: close to something
a long way from something

look.title: Where Is the Cat?
look.text: Look at a picture of a yard. A cat sits on the left. It is near a tree. A dog sits on the right. It is far from the tree. A ball sits in the middle. The cat is close to the ball. The dog is not.
look.prompt: Is the dog near the tree or far from it? How do you know?

check.q: Near means what?
check.why: Near means close. Far means a long way off.

check.q: On the treasure map, the star was far from what?
check.why: The star was near the rug and far from the door.

check.q: A friend says, "Turn left at the door." What kind of word is left?
check.why: Left and right are direction words. They tell which way to go.

lessons.title: North, South, East and West
lessons.mainIdea: North, south, east and west are the four main directions on a map.
reading: Left and right can change. Turn around, and left is now right! So map makers use four words that never change. *North*. *South*. East. West. On most maps, north is at the top.
Here is a trick. The sun comes up in the east. It goes down in the west. Face the sunrise. East is in front of you. West is behind you. North is on your left. South is on your right.
Maps often have a small cross with the letters N, S, E, W. Find it. Then you know which way is north. Then you can find every other direction too.

words.d: the direction at the top of most maps
the direction at the bottom of most maps

look.title: The Sun in the Morning
look.text: It is morning. Ana stands in her yard. The sun is just coming up. She faces it. Now east is in front of her. Her house is behind her. Her left hand points to the park.
look.prompt: Which direction is the park from Ana? Which direction is her house?

check.q: On most maps, which direction is at the top?
check.why: On most maps, north is at the top. South is at the bottom.

check.q: Where does the sun come up?
check.why: The sun comes up in the east. It goes down in the west.

check.q: Why do map makers use north and south instead of left and right?
choices: They never change when you turn
check.why: Left and right change when you turn around. North, south, east and west stay the same.

lessons.title: The Globe Is a Model of Earth
lessons.mainIdea: A globe is a round model of Earth that shows land and water.
reading: Earth is very big. It is round like a ball. We cannot see all of it at once. So people made a *globe*. A globe is a small model of Earth. You can spin it. You can hold it.
Look at a globe. Most of it is blue. Blue means water. The big blue parts are oceans. The green and brown parts are *land*. There is more water than land on Earth.
A flat map of the world shows the same thing. Blue is water. Green or brown is land. Rivers are thin blue lines. Lakes are blue shapes with land all around.

words.d: a round model of Earth
the dry parts of Earth, where we walk and build

look.title: Water and Land on Earth
look.prompt: Are there more water parts or more land parts? What color will most of a globe be?

check.q: What is a globe?
choices: A kind of ball for games
check.why: A globe is a small round model of Earth. You can spin it and hold it.

check.q: On a globe, what does blue mean?
check.why: Blue shows water. The big blue parts are oceans.

check.q: Which is there more of on Earth?
check.why: Most of a globe is blue. There is more water than land on Earth.

lessons.title: Finding Our Home
lessons.mainIdea: We live in Chicago, in the state of Illinois, in the United States.
reading: Find the United States on a globe. It is a big country. It is in the top half of the globe. It has an ocean on its left side and an ocean on its right side. That is our *country*.
The United States has fifty *states*. One is Illinois. Find it in the middle of the country. It is tall and thin. A big lake touches its top right corner. That lake is Lake Michigan.
Chicago is a city in Illinois. It sits right on Lake Michigan. On a map, it is a dot near the top of the state. Many people live in that dot. Maybe you do too.

words.d: a big land with its own name and its own leaders
one part of the United States, like Illinois

look.title: Zooming In
look.text: Start with the whole globe. Find the United States. Now zoom in. Find Illinois in the middle. Now zoom in more. Find the big lake in the corner. Find the dot on the lake. That dot is Chicago. Zoom in again. Somewhere in that dot is your school.
look.prompt: Which is bigger, Illinois or Chicago? How can you tell from the map?

check.q: Illinois is a…
check.why: Illinois is one of the fifty states in the United States.

check.q: What big lake touches Chicago?
check.why: Chicago sits right on Lake Michigan. The lake touches the top right corner of Illinois.

check.q: Which is the biggest?
check.why: The United States is a country. Illinois is one state inside it. Chicago is one city inside Illinois.

lessons.title: A Route to School
lessons.mainIdea: A route is the path you take to get from one place to another.
reading: Leo walks to school. He leaves his door. He turns right. He walks past the store. He turns left at the park. He crosses the street at the light. Then he is at school. That is his *route*.
A route is the path from one place to another. You can draw it on a map. Start at home. Draw a line. Follow the streets. End at school. Mark the turns.
A good route map tells you where to turn. It shows the things you pass. The store. The park. The light. Those things help you know you are going the right way.

words.d: the path you take from one place to another

look.title: Two Ways to the Park
look.text: Mia can go two ways to the park. Way one: go straight up her street. It is short. Way two: go past the library, then turn left. It is longer. But it has a sidewalk the whole way. Mia's mom picks way two.
look.prompt: Why might Mia's mom pick the longer route?

check.q: What is a route?
choices: A path from one place to another
check.why: A route is the path you take to get from one place to another.

check.q: Where did Leo turn left?
check.why: Leo turned right at his door. He turned left at the park.

check.q: What helps you know you are going the right way?
choices: The things you pass, like the store
check.why: A good route map shows the things you pass. Seeing them tells you that you are on the right path.

review.q: A map is a drawing of a place from…
review.why: A map shows a place from above, the way a bird sees it.

review.q: What tells you what a star on a map means?
review.why: The key lists each symbol and tells what it means.

review.q: The sun comes up in the…
review.why: The sun comes up in the east and goes down in the west.
A globe is a small round model of Earth. Most of it is blue for water.

review.q: Chicago is a city in which state?
review.why: Chicago is a city in the state of Illinois. The United States is the country.

review.q: On a route map, what should you mark?
choices: The turns and the things you pass
review.why: A route map shows where to turn and what you pass along the way.

chapters.title: Land, Water and Weather Where We Live
chapters.bigQuestion: How does a place shape the people who live there, and how do people shape the place?

story.title: Out the Car Window
story.kicker: Grandpa's farm is far from Chicago. Watch what changes on the long drive south.
paragraphs: Nia climbs into the back seat. Her family is driving to Grandpa's farm. It is far to the south. Out the window she sees tall buildings. She sees buses and trains. She sees a slice of blue. That is Lake Michigan.
The car gets on the highway. The tall buildings get small. Then they are gone. Now Nia sees houses with yards. Then big stores. Then fewer and fewer houses. The land gets very flat.
Soon there are fields on both sides. Green corn goes on and on. A red barn sits far away. A tractor moves slowly. The sky looks bigger here. Nia can see all the way to the edge of the land.

The car turns onto a dirt road. Dust flies up. Grandpa waves from the porch. "Same state as Chicago," he says. "Just a different place." Nia looks around. No lake. No tall buildings. Only fields and sky.
story.think: What did Nia see in the city that she did not see at the farm? What did she see at the farm that was not in the city?

lessons.title: Hills and Plains
lessons.mainIdea: Land can be high and bumpy, like a hill, or low and flat, like a plain.
reading: Land is not all the same. Some land goes up. A *hill* is a bump of land that rises up. You walk up one side. You walk down the other. A very big, tall hill is a mountain.
Some land is flat. A *plain* is a big piece of flat land. You can see a long way across it. There are no bumps to block your view. Nia saw a plain from the car.
Both hills and plains are called landforms. A landform is a shape the land makes. Look out a window. Is the land near you flat? Or does it go up and down?

words.d: a bump of land that rises up
a big piece of flat land

look.title: The Sled Hill
look.text: It snowed last night. Kids drag sleds to the park. There is one big hill. They climb up. They zoom down. Next to the park is a flat field. Nobody sleds there. The sleds just sit still on the flat snow.
look.prompt: Why do the kids sled on the hill and not on the field?

check.q: What is a hill?
choices: A bump of land that rises up
A big piece of flat land
check.why: A hill is a bump of land. You walk up one side and down the other.

check.q: On a plain, why can you see a long way?
choices: The land is flat with no bumps
check.why: A plain is flat. Nothing rises up to block your view.

check.q: A hill and a plain are both…
check.why: A landform is a shape the land makes. Hills and plains are both landforms.

lessons.title: Rivers, Lakes and the Ocean
lessons.mainIdea: Water on Earth comes in rivers, lakes and the huge, salty ocean.
reading: A *river* is water that moves. It flows from high land to low land. It is long and thin. On a map, it is a thin blue line. Boats can ride on a river.

A *lake* is water with land all around it. It does not flow away. Lake Michigan is a lake next to Chicago. It is so big you cannot see the other side. But it is still a lake. Its water is fresh, not salty.

The *ocean* is the biggest water of all. It is salty. It goes on for days and days. Illinois does not touch an ocean. The United States touches two. One is on the left side of the map. One is on the right.

words.d: water that flows along in a long, thin path
water with land all around it
the biggest, saltiest body of water on Earth

look.title: How Big Is the Water?
look.cite: standard rounded figures, made simple for comparing
look.prompt: Which one could you walk around in a day? Which one could you never walk around?

check.q: Which water flows from high land to low land?
check.why: A river is moving water. It flows downhill in a long, thin path.

check.q: What is Lake Michigan?
check.why: Lake Michigan has land all around it. It is a lake, even though it is huge.

check.q: Which water is salty?
check.why: The ocean is salty. Lake Michigan and rivers are fresh water.

lessons.title: Flat Illinois
lessons.mainIdea: Most of Illinois is flat prairie land, and much of it is now farmland.
reading: Long ago, most of Illinois was *prairie*. A prairie is a plain covered in tall grass. The grass could grow taller than a person. Wind made it wave like water. Illinois is still called the Prairie State.
Today most of that prairie is *farmland*. Farmers plowed the grass under. They planted corn and soybeans. When Nia looked out the car window, she saw fields, not tall grass.
Illinois has water too. The Mississippi River runs along its west edge. The Illinois River flows through the middle. Lake Michigan touches the top right corner. Chicago sits on that lake.

words.d: a flat land covered in tall grass
land where people grow crops or raise animals

look.title: Tall Grass, Then Corn
look.text: Picture a field two hundred years ago. Grass grows higher than your head. Wind blows and the grass waves. Now picture the same field today. Rows of corn stand in straight lines. A tractor rolls between them. Same flat land. Different plants.
look.prompt: What did people do to change the field from grass to corn?

check.q: What is a prairie?
check.why: A prairie is a plain covered in tall grass. Illinois is called the Prairie State.

check.q: What grows on most Illinois farmland today?
check.why: Farmers plowed the prairie and planted corn and soybeans.

check.q: Which river runs along the west edge of Illinois?
check.why: The Mississippi River runs along the west edge of Illinois.

lessons.title: Four Seasons in Illinois
lessons.mainIdea: Illinois has four seasons, and the weather changes with each one.
reading: *Weather* is what the sky is doing today. Sunny. Rainy. Windy. Snowy. In Illinois, the weather changes a lot. That is because we have four *seasons*.

Winter is cold. Snow falls in Chicago. Lake Michigan can get ice near the shore. Spring is wet and cool. Rain falls. Plants wake up. Summer is hot. Corn grows tall. Fall is cool again. Leaves turn red and gold and drop.
The seasons go in a circle. Winter, spring, summer, fall. Then winter again. Every year, the same order. Farmers plant in spring and pick in fall because of this.

words.d: what the sky is doing: sun, rain, wind, snow
one of the four parts of the year: winter, spring, summer, fall

look.title: A Chicago Year
look.unit: degrees, about, on a warm afternoon
look.prompt: Which month is hottest? Which is coldest? What would you wear in each?

check.q: How many seasons does Illinois have?
check.why: Illinois has four seasons: winter, spring, summer and fall.

check.q: Which season comes right after summer?
check.why: The seasons go winter, spring, summer, fall. Fall comes after summer.

check.q: When do Illinois farmers plant corn?
check.why: Farmers plant in spring, when the ground warms up. They pick in fall.

lessons.title: What Weather Makes Us Do
lessons.mainIdea: The weather shapes what people wear and what they do.
reading: It is January in Chicago. Nia puts on a coat, a hat and mittens. She walks to school on a shoveled sidewalk. At recess, she stays inside. It is too cold to play out.
It is July. Nia wears shorts and a T-shirt. She runs through a sprinkler. Her family goes to the beach on Lake Michigan. The city opens the pools.
Weather changes what we wear. It changes what we do. It changes work too. Snowplows run in winter. Farmers work the fields in summer. People *adapt*. That means they change to fit the weather.

words.d: to change what you do so it fits the place or the weather

look.title: Two Backpacks
look.text: Look at two backpacks by the door. One has mittens, a scarf and a thermos of hot cocoa. The other has a water bottle, sunscreen and a swimsuit. Both belong to the same kid.
look.prompt: Which backpack is for winter? Which is for summer? How do you know?

check.q: Why does Nia stay inside at recess in January?
choices: The playground is closed for good
check.why: In January, Chicago is very cold. Kids often stay inside at recess.

check.q: What does adapt mean?
choices: To change to fit the weather
check.why: To adapt is to change what you do so it fits the place or the weather.

check.q: Which job is a winter job in Chicago?
check.why: Snowplows run in winter, when snow falls. Beaches and sprinklers are for summer.

lessons.title: People Change Places
lessons.mainIdea: People change the land by building roads, planting crops and digging ponds.
reading: Grandpa's farm was not always a farm. Long ago it was tall grass. People cut the grass. They plowed the dirt. They planted corn. They built a barn and a house. They changed the place.
People change places every day. They *build* roads over fields. They dig ponds so cows can drink. They put up houses and stores. In Chicago, people even made a river flow the other way, long ago.
Look around your neighborhood. The sidewalk. The street. The school. The playground. People made all of that. Under it all is the land that was there first.

words.d: to make something new, like a road or a house

look.title: The Empty Lot
look.text: There is an empty lot on the corner. It has dirt and weeds. One spring, people come with shovels. They dig out rocks. They bring in good soil. They plant tomatoes and beans. They put up a little fence. Now it is a garden.
look.prompt: How did the people change the lot? What was there before?

check.q: What did people do to turn prairie into a farm?
choices: Plowed the grass and planted crops
Waited for the grass to change
check.why: People cut and plowed the tall grass. Then they planted corn and built a barn.

check.q: Which one is a way people change a place?
choices: A road is built over a field
check.why: Building a road is something people do. Rain and snow are weather, not people.

check.q: Why do farmers dig ponds?
choices: To grow corn in the water
check.why: Farmers dig ponds so cows and other animals have water to drink.

lessons.title: Places Shape People
lessons.mainIdea: The land and water of a place shape the jobs and lives of the people there.
reading: A town by the ocean often has many fishers. The water is right there. Boats go out in the morning. They come back full of fish. The place gave people that job.
A town on the flat prairie often has many farmers. The soil is rich. The land is flat and easy to plow. Grandpa's town is a farm town. Its stores sell seeds and tractor parts.
Chicago grew big because of Lake Michigan. Boats could bring things in and out. Then trains met the boats. The place made the city. So places shape people, and people shape places.

words.d: a person whose job is catching fish

look.title: Two Towns
look.text: Town A sits by the sea. Its main street has a boat shop, a net shop and a fish market. Town B sits on flat farmland. Its main street has a seed store, a tractor shop and a grain tower. Each town looks different.
look.prompt: Why does Town A have a net shop and Town B have a seed store?

check.q: Why does a town by the ocean have many fishers?
choices: The water and fish are right there
It gets a lot of snow
check.why: The ocean is right there. So many people in that town catch fish for a living.

check.q: What kind of town is Grandpa's town?
check.why: Grandpa's town is on flat prairie with rich soil. It is a farm town.

check.q: What helped Chicago grow into a big city?
check.why: Boats on Lake Michigan carried things in and out. Later trains met the boats. The city grew.

lessons.title: Taking Care of a Place
lessons.mainIdea: People can keep a place healthy by picking up litter, saving water and planting trees.
reading: A place takes care of us. It gives us water, food and air. We can take care of it too. Start with *litter*. Litter is trash left on the ground. Pick it up. Put it in a can.
Save water. Turn off the tap while you brush your teeth. Lake Michigan gives Chicago its drinking water. Keep trash out of the lake and the rivers. Clean water is for everyone.
Plant trees. Trees give shade in hot summers. They give homes to birds. Their roots hold the dirt in place when it rains. One kid, one tree, one clean park. That is how you care for a place.

words.d: trash left on the ground where it does not belong

look.title: Park Cleanup Day
look.prompt: What will the park look like next summer because of this day?

check.q: What is litter?
check.why: Litter is trash left where it does not belong. Pick it up and put it in a can.

check.q: Where does Chicago get its drinking water?
check.why: Lake Michigan gives Chicago its drinking water. That is one reason to keep it clean.

check.q: How do trees help a place?
choices: They give shade and homes for birds
check.why: Trees give shade, homes for birds, and roots that hold the dirt in place.

review.q: Which is a big piece of flat land?
review.why: A plain is flat land. A hill rises up. A river is water.

choices: Fresh water with land all around
review.why: Lake Michigan is a huge lake. Its water is fresh and land surrounds it.

review.q: Why is Illinois called the Prairie State?
choices: It was once mostly tall grass on flat land
review.why: Long ago most of Illinois was prairie, flat land with tall grass.

review.q: Which season in Illinois is hot, with tall corn?
review.why: Summer is hot. Corn grows tall then. Farmers pick it in fall.

review.q: Which is an example of people changing a place?
choices: Building a road over a field
review.why: People build roads. Leaves and snow are things nature does.

review.q: Which is a way to take care of a place?
choices: Pick up litter and plant a tree
review.why: Picking up litter, saving water and planting trees keep a place healthy.
